abstract: This paper examines how technological progress affects wage outcomes depending on the nature of innovation. The authors argue that when capital and labor are gross complements—an empirically plausible scenario—capital-augmenting innovation is necessary to raise wages, whereas labor-augmenting innovation may have different distributional effects. The work addresses how the direction of technological progress can be steered to achieve desired labor market outcomes.
keyFindings: Capital and labor are empirically plausible gross complements in production
Capital-augmenting innovation is required to raise wages when capital and labor are gross complements
Labor-augmenting innovation alone is insufficient for wage increases under these conditions
qualifiers: The findings are described as applying to 'the empirically plausible case' of capital-labor complementarity, suggesting this is based on empirical evidence, though the specific evidence basis and scope are not detailed in the provided excerpt.
